toc.title: Accessing safety: two things you need
When you live in a traumatized state

blocks.p: What is polyvagal safety, and how do you use it? The second half of that question is a little misleading, because the polyvagal state of safety is not something that can be used. Not exactly. It's not a tool. It's not a technique. It's not a fidget.

The Polyvagal Theory is dense and complex. It's not easily understood the first time, so you might be looking for more information, and specifically: what the heck is this safety stuff? And how do I use it? That's a great question, but it's actually kind of the wrong question. So let's figure out first what polyvagal safety is.

Polyvagal safety is a reference to biology, and all the states are. They're first and foremost a reference to biology. We're not just talking about feelings. We're not just talking about "trauma responses." We are talking about biology.

So when you hear "polyvagal safety," that is specifically referring to the ventral vagal pathways of the autonomic nervous system, to put it simply. When these pathways are active, a mammal is able to connect with other mammals. It leads to co-regulation, safe connection, relationships, families, nurturance. It's responsible for all of that and more.
Polyvagal safety allows you to socially engage. It allows you to provide cues of safety to another, and that's called co-regulation. When you're in your safety state, you can:

ul: Use vocal prosody, a more singsongy quality to your voice.
Listen, and squint your eyes so those crinkles form at the sides of them.
Get close to somebody and hug.

blocks.p: There are all these wonderful abilities that come along with the polyvagal state of safety and social engagement that aren't accessible when you don't have access to that state.
When it's active, the safety state also lets you access other states and create mixed states.

There are three primary polyvagal states: safety, flight or fight, and shutdown. When they interact, or mix, they create mixed states, just like primary colors mix to create mixed colors. Red and blue make purple. When the safety state is active, it can mix with flight, fight, or shutdown and create something different.
Flight and fight get repurposed for play. Mobilization plus safety equals play.

Shutdown is immobilization, like a death feign or collapse. When safety is active along with it, it becomes stillness: the capacity to be still, to self-reflect, to sit in class. You might be using some stillness right now, sitting in your chair at work.
When the safety state isn't active, those defensive states are just flight and fight, or just shutdown. They're their own primary states. But when safety is active, they become something else.

blocks.h: Accessing safety: two things you need

blocks.p: So the next question becomes: "Awesome, Justin. How do I access my safety state? How do I become more in my safety state?" There are a couple of basic things that need to be present.
1. Environmental safety. Actual, factual, literal safety. You need to be free from actual danger to your person, your body.

This also includes a more subtle form of safety. You might not have a clear and present danger, but there can be things in the environment that take you a little out of your safety state, or challenge your capacity to access it or stay in it. These are passive cues of danger you otherwise wouldn't notice: the hum of a refrigerator, bright fluorescent lighting, coldness. Temperature has a lot to do with our neuroceptions of safety or danger.
2. Interpersonal safety. Again, I mean literal safety. When you're with somebody who is actually a safe person, who's not attacking you, that's kind of necessary to access your safety state.

Co-regulation is the ability to receive cues of safety from a safe mammal. It could be a human, or it could be a pet: when they look you in the eyes, or come up and cuddle with you, and it helps you feel better. That's co-regulation. It helps you get out of your own defensive state, up your [polyvagal ladder](piece:autonomic-nervous-system) into safety.
These two pieces, actual safety in the environment and actual safety with people, are absolutely essential for accessing your polyvagal state of safety.
No one has a perfectly cozy, perfectly warm environment or relationship. If you do, congratulations. We're not looking for perfection. We're looking for good enough.

Maybe your environment isn't perfect, with the right wall color and the right heaviness of blanket and the right scent and the right lighting. But maybe you get one or two of those environmental safety cues just right, and that's good enough to help you access your safety state.

Deb Dana said it simply when she was on the podcast: "There have to be more cues of safety than danger in order for me to move into ventral." ([Episode 29](https://player.captivate.fm/episode/f8b9643c-28f8-4185-9525-8b4e6301516c))

Likewise, maybe you're with someone who isn't a perfect co-regulator, but they're doing a good enough job, or you can tell they're really trying to connect with you in their own way. Maybe that's enough to help you access your own safety state.

blocks.h: When you live in a traumatized state

blocks.p: If you live in a traumatized state, it's going to be a lot more difficult to access the safety state and remain in it. It's actually going to be a pretty significant challenge. Those safety pathways may simply not be developed enough yet. Yet. I'm emphasizing the word yet.

Feeling your safety state might actually be really uncomfortable. I had a session with a teenage client who was able to climb out of shutdown up into fight and actually feel it. They were awesome. They moved through flight and up into their safety state. When they got there, they had a little difficulty hanging onto it, and they noticed thoughts of self-sabotage entering their consciousness. "Well, can I keep it up?" Or, "Why even bother? You'll end up failing anyway."
Accessing the safety state is great, and we have to do it, in order to keep practicing accessing it so it's easier the next time. But really, you're building the strength of those safety pathways.

So the building is really important. It's not just about accessing it. It's not about resetting the vagus nerve, whatever that means. It's not about hacking something or other. It's not about doing the right technique to reset or rewire, or whatever the popular terminology is at the moment. It's about the continual practice of accessing your safety state.

And the way you know you're there is that you feel it. You'll feel more connection, more patience or empathy, calm. You might feel an impulse to be close to others, or to look inward and be more curious about what you have inside of you. Those are your indicators that you're in your safety pathways.

So polyvagal safety is not something to be used. It's not something you can consciously turn off and on, and I don't encourage you to think about it that way. It's something to be developed. It's something you practice, and maybe build the strength of. That might be a better way to put it. I encourage you to think of it as a long process, a journey of getting unstuck. It's not a one-time thing. It has to happen slowly, over time.

blocks.why: This article is about practicing. This is the practice built from your check-ins.

blocks.p: You can definitely increase the chances of your safety state being active. One way is by controlling the factors in your home. Maybe there's some lighting you can switch up. Maybe you can add a comfy blanket, or a scent from a candle you like. In the fall, I love the smell of pumpkin, and that's something we have going in our home.

You could also do more active things, like playing with your kids or creating something with art. There may be things you can actively do and really mindfully experience. Once you're doing them, what does it feel like? What does it feel like to make eye contact with your pet? If you can do it mindfully, that really helps you practice being in that state and build the strength of those pathways.
